definitions.definition: Abetment, as used in the Prevention of Corruption Act, refers to the act of instigating, engaging in conspiracy with, or intentionally aiding any person in committing an offence punishable under the Act, as defined under Sections 107–109 of the Indian Penal Code. Under Section 12, a person who abets any such offence is liable to punishment regardless of whether the principal offence is actually committed in consequence of that abetment.
definitions.plain_english: Abetment means helping, encouraging, or conspiring with someone to commit a corruption-related crime, even if the crime never actually happens. If you advise, assist, or team up with a public servant to take a bribe or commit any other corrupt act, you are guilty of abetment. You can be punished for this even if the actual corrupt act was never carried out.
real_world_examples: A private contractor in Mumbai approaches a PWD officer and repeatedly persuades him to approve inflated bills in exchange for a kickback, even though the officer ultimately refuses — the contractor is guilty of abetment.

A middleman in Delhi acts as an intermediary, collecting money from a job-seeker and promising to deliver it to a government clerk to secure a posting, thereby actively facilitating the bribe transaction — this constitutes abetment.

A company's HR manager in Bengaluru instructs a junior employee to deliver cash in an envelope to a municipal inspector to expedite a trade licence approval — the HR manager abets the offence of bribery.

A chartered accountant in Chennai knowingly prepares false balance sheets and coaches a client on how to offer illegal gratification to an income tax officer to reduce an assessment — the accountant is guilty of abetment of the bribery offence.

A politician's aide in Hyderabad arranges meetings and facilitates communication between a land developer and a revenue official, knowing that bribes are being negotiated, without personally handing over any money — this indirect facilitation amounts to abetment.

A senior officer in a state PSU pressures a subordinate public servant to accept a gift from a vendor, threatening adverse consequences if refused — the senior officer abets the offence under the Act.
what_it_covers: A private individual who instigates or persuades a public servant to commit an offence under the Act, even if the public servant refuses.
A person who intentionally aids the commission of a corruption offence by providing money, logistics, information, or other assistance to the principal offender.
Two or more persons who conspire together to commit an offence under the Act, where at least one takes a step in furtherance of that conspiracy.
A middleman who acts as a conduit between a bribe-giver and a public servant, facilitating the corrupt transaction.
A superior officer who coerces or encourages a subordinate public servant to engage in corrupt conduct.
what_it_excludes: A person who merely has knowledge of a corruption offence but takes no active steps to instigate, aid, or conspire in its commission.
Innocent third parties such as banks or couriers who unknowingly and without intent facilitate a transaction that turns out to be part of a corrupt arrangement.
A public servant who is the principal accused and directly commits the primary offence — they are charged under the substantive sections of the Act, not under Section 12 for abetment.
Acts done under duress or coercion without any voluntary intent to assist or encourage the commission of the offence.
Mere association or social interaction with a person who commits a corruption offence, without any intentional facilitation or encouragement.
definitions.why_it_matters: Section 12 creates independent criminal liability for abettors, meaning a person can be convicted and sentenced to a minimum of three years and up to seven years of imprisonment plus fine even if the principal corruption offence was never completed. This provision ensures that intermediaries, fixers, instigators, and conspirators who facilitate corruption cannot escape punishment on the technicality that the primary offence did not ultimately occur.

definitions.definition: An 'associated person' in the context of the Prevention of Corruption Act refers to a person who performs services for or on behalf of a commercial organisation, including as an employee, agent, or subsidiary, and whose acts of bribery or corrupt conduct in connection with those services are attributable to the commercial organisation for the purposes of establishing liability under the Act.
definitions.plain_english: An associated person is someone who works for, represents, or acts on behalf of a company or business organisation in some capacity. This could be an employee, a contractor, an agent, or even another company working under the main organisation. The key point is that if this person pays a bribe or acts corruptly while doing work for the organisation, the organisation itself can be held responsible.
real_world_examples: A sales agent hired by a Mumbai-based pharmaceutical company to obtain government drug approvals pays a bribe to a public servant at the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation — the agent is an associated person and the company can face liability under Section 9.

A third-party logistics contractor engaged by a Chennai export firm bribes a customs official at Chennai Port to clear goods without proper inspection — the contractor, acting on behalf of the firm, qualifies as an associated person.

An employee of a Delhi-based infrastructure company pays an unofficial gratification to a government engineer of the National Highways Authority of India to secure a road construction contract — the employee is an associated person and the company is exposed to corporate liability.

A subsidiary company of a Bengaluru IT firm offers undue advantage to an official of a public sector undertaking to win a software procurement deal — the subsidiary, performing services on behalf of the parent firm, is treated as an associated person of the commercial organisation.

A public relations consultant retained by a Kolkata manufacturing company pays money to a municipal officer to fast-track factory licensing approvals — the consultant acting as an agent on behalf of the company constitutes an associated person under the Act.
what_it_covers: Employees of a commercial organisation who pay bribes or offer undue advantage to public servants while carrying out their duties for the organisation.
Independent agents, consultants, or contractors who perform services on behalf of a commercial organisation and engage in corrupt conduct in connection with those services.
Subsidiary companies or sister entities that perform services for a parent commercial organisation and whose officers commit bribery attributable to the parent organisation.
Business partners or joint venture participants acting under the direction or authority of a commercial organisation while engaging in corrupt practices to benefit that organisation.
what_it_excludes: Public servants acting in their official capacity, who are governed by separate provisions of the Act and are not considered 'associated persons' of a commercial organisation.
Individuals who act entirely independently and not in any capacity connected to the commercial organisation, even if the organisation incidentally benefits from their corrupt act.
Shareholders or passive investors of a commercial organisation who do not perform any services for or on behalf of the organisation and have no operational role.

Persons who were formerly associated with the commercial organisation but had completely severed their relationship prior to the commission of the offence and were not acting on its behalf at the relevant time.
definitions.why_it_matters: The classification of a person as an 'associated person' is the foundational trigger for corporate liability under Section 9 of the Act — if the person who committed bribery is found to be an associated person, the commercial organisation itself becomes guilty of an offence and liable to be fined. Without this link, the organisation cannot be prosecuted, making this definition central to whether corporate criminal responsibility attaches.

definitions.definition: For the purposes of Section 17C of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 'attachment' shall include temporarily assuming the custody, possession and/or control of such property. Where it is not practicable to seize such property, an order of attachment directs that such property shall not be transferred or otherwise dealt with, except with the prior permission of the Investigating Officer or the Designated Authority.
definitions.plain_english: Attachment means officially taking temporary control over a property that is suspected to have been acquired through corruption, so that the owner cannot sell, transfer, or misuse it during an investigation. If physically taking the property is not possible, a legal order is issued forbidding the owner from doing anything with it without official permission. This is a preventive step taken before a court decides whether the property should be permanently taken away.
real_world_examples: A Deputy Superintendent of Police investigating a corrupt PWD officer in Jammu finds that the officer purchased three commercial shops in Srinagar using bribe money; the officer issues an attachment order preventing the sale or mortgage of those shops while the investigation is ongoing.

An Anti-Corruption Bureau officer discovers that a government contractor who paid bribes to secure tenders has deposited large sums in fixed deposit accounts with a nationalised bank; an attachment order is issued temporarily assuming control of those fixed deposits so they cannot be prematurely withdrawn.

A senior revenue official in Jammu & Kashmir is found to own a farmhouse disproportionate to his known sources of income; since the property cannot be physically seized, an attachment order is served directing that the farmhouse shall not be sold, gifted, or mortgaged without the Designated Authority's permission.

During investigation of a forest department officer for criminal misconduct, the Anti-Corruption Bureau identifies a fleet of luxury vehicles registered in the name of his spouse; the Investigating Officer, with the Director's written approval, issues an attachment order temporarily assuming custody of those vehicles.

A public servant in a procurement department is found to have invested bribe proceeds in equity shares held in a demat account; an attachment order is served on the stockbroker directing that the shares shall not be transferred, pledged, or liquidated pending the Designated Authority's confirmation within thirty days.
what_it_covers: Immovable properties such as land, buildings, or commercial premises suspected to have been acquired through criminal misconduct, where a formal order directing non-transfer is issued because physical seizure is impracticable.
Movable properties including vehicles, jewellery, cash, or securities over which the Investigating Officer temporarily assumes custody, possession, and/or control by virtue of an attachment order.

Bank accounts, fixed deposits, and financial instruments linked to proceeds of corruption, which are frozen so that the account holder cannot operate or withdraw from them without the Designated Authority's prior permission.
Properties registered in the name of associates or family members of the accused public servant where there is reason to believe they were acquired using proceeds of criminal misconduct.

Any property in respect of which the Investigating Officer has reason to believe it is likely to be transferred or dealt with to defeat prosecution, attracting the provisional ninety-day attachment under the proviso to Section 17C(1).
what_it_excludes: Permanent confiscation or forfeiture of property, which requires a separate order by the Special Court under Section 17D and is not achieved merely by attachment.
Properties acquired through legitimate and verifiable known sources of income that bear no nexus to any act of criminal misconduct under Section 5 of the Act.
Attachment proceedings governed exclusively by the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002, which are expressly saved from the operation of Section 18A and follow a distinct statutory regime.

Bona fide transferees who have already acquired valid title to a property before the attachment order is served, provided their transaction is not tainted by the criminal misconduct under investigation.
Perishable property that cannot practically be held under attachment for extended periods and must instead be dealt with through a sale order under Section 17D read with Section 459 CrPC.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a measure qualifies as 'attachment' determines whether the Investigating Officer has authority to temporarily assume control of suspected corruption proceeds and whether the Designated Authority's confirmation or revocation within thirty days is mandatory; failure to properly invoke attachment strips the prosecution of the ability to preserve assets for eventual forfeiture under Section 17D and triggers the right of appeal by the aggrieved person to the Special Court.

definitions.definition: The expression 'bank' shall have the meaning assigned to it in the Bankers' Books Evidence Act, 1891 (18 of 1891), as applied within the context of Section 18 of the Prevention of Corruption Act for the purpose of inspecting bankers' books relating to accounts of persons suspected of committing offences under the Act.
definitions.plain_english: A 'bank' here means any bank as defined under the Bankers' Books Evidence Act, 1891 — broadly covering all banks whose account records can be legally inspected during a corruption investigation. When a police officer suspects corruption, they can compel such a bank to allow inspection of its records. The bank is legally obligated to assist the investigating officer in this process.
real_world_examples: A Superintendent of Police investigating a bribery case against a government official in Maharashtra directs the State Bank of India branch in Pune to allow inspection of the official's savings and fixed deposit accounts under Section 18.

During a disproportionate assets inquiry against a senior IAS officer in Delhi, an investigating officer inspects the HDFC Bank accounts of the officer's spouse suspected of holding funds on the officer's behalf.

A CBI officer investigating a public works contractor for corrupt payments inspects the ICICI Bank current account of the contractor's firm to obtain certified copies of entries showing suspicious fund transfers.

In a case involving a public servant in Telangana suspected of accepting bribes, the Investigating Officer inspects the Punjab National Bank accounts of a third party suspected to be holding money on behalf of the accused public servant.

A police officer of or above the rank of Superintendent of Police authorises inspection of Axis Bank records of a municipal corporation official in Chennai whose accounts show unexplained large deposits following a tender award.
what_it_covers: All banks as defined under the Bankers' Books Evidence Act, 1891, including nationalised banks, scheduled commercial banks, and cooperative banks covered under that Act.
Private sector banks such as HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank, and Axis Bank whose books are subject to inspection during a corruption investigation under Section 18.

Any bank holding accounts of persons suspected to be holding money on behalf of a corruption accused, making them liable to assist the investigating officer even if they are not the primary account holder under investigation.
what_it_excludes: Non-banking financial companies (NBFCs) that are not classified as 'banks' under the Bankers' Books Evidence Act, 1891, and therefore fall outside the scope of this definition.
Informal money-lending entities, chit fund companies, or hawala operators that do not qualify as a 'bank' under the Bankers' Books Evidence Act, 1891.
Digital payment platforms or fintech entities that do not hold a banking licence and are not covered under the Bankers' Books Evidence Act, 1891, unless they operate under a bank umbrella entity.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an entity qualifies as a 'bank' under this definition determines whether a police officer can compel it under Section 18 to produce account records and certified copies during a corruption investigation — non-compliance by a qualifying bank constitutes obstruction of the investigation, while entities outside this definition cannot be legally compelled under this provision. The definition thus directly triggers the obligation of financial cooperation and the investigative powers of the police in corruption cases.

definitions.definition: The expression 'bankers' books' shall have the meaning assigned to it in the Bankers' Books Evidence Act, 1891 (18 of 1891), which includes ledgers, day-books, cash-books, account-books and all other books used in the ordinary course of the banking business, whether kept in written form or as printouts of data stored in any form of electromagnetic data storage device.
definitions.plain_english: Bankers' books are the official financial records that a bank maintains as part of its regular business operations, such as ledgers, account registers, and transaction logs. Under the Prevention of Corruption Act, a senior police officer can inspect these records to trace money linked to corruption offences. They include both physical paper records and digital/electronic records stored by banks.
real_world_examples: A Superintendent of Police investigating a bribery case against a PWD contractor in Maharashtra inspects the contractor's SBI savings and current account ledgers to trace large unexplained deposits made shortly after a government contract was awarded.

The CBI, while probing a disproportionate assets case against a senior IAS officer in Delhi, obtains certified copies of entries from his HDFC Bank account books to establish deposits inconsistent with his known salary income.
A police officer authorized by the SP inspects the bankers' books of a hawala operator in Hyderabad who is suspected of holding money on behalf of a corrupt municipal official under investigation.

During a Prevention of Corruption case in Punjab, investigators inspect the fixed deposit registers and loan account books of a co-operative bank to determine whether a public servant secretly holds assets through a benami account maintained there.

In a Chennai corruption case, the Directorate of Vigilance and Anti-Corruption inspects digitally stored account statements and transaction logs (electronic bankers' books) of a private bank to trace kickbacks paid to a state government procurement officer.
what_it_covers: Physical ledgers, day-books, cash-books, and account-books maintained by a bank in the ordinary course of its banking business.
Printouts or copies of data stored in electromagnetic or digital data storage devices used by banks to record transactions, including core banking system records.
Records of accounts held by persons suspected of corruption as well as accounts of third parties suspected of holding money on their behalf.
Both demand deposit account registers and fixed deposit records, loan account books, and any other books forming part of routine banking operations.
Entries in bankers' books of scheduled commercial banks, co-operative banks, and any institution defined as a 'bank' under the Bankers' Books Evidence Act, 1891.
what_it_excludes: Internal administrative files, board minutes, or policy documents of a bank that are not used in the ordinary course of banking business transactions.
Records or documents maintained by non-banking financial companies (NBFCs), chit funds, or money lenders that do not fall within the definition of 'bank' under the Bankers' Books Evidence Act, 1891.
Personal diaries, notebooks, or informal records kept by bank employees that are not part of the official books of the bank.
Records of foreign banks maintained exclusively outside India and not forming part of the Indian branch's books.
Insurance company account records or stock-broker transaction records, even if kept in book form, as these entities are not 'banks' within the meaning of the Bankers' Books Evidence Act, 1891.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a document qualifies as a 'bankers' book' determines whether a police officer has the statutory power under Section 18 to inspect and obtain certified copies of it without further court process, and whether the bank is legally bound to cooperate; if the record does not fall within this definition, the officer cannot compel access under this provision, potentially obstructing the financial investigation of corruption offences.

definitions.definition: A bona fide transferee is a person who holds or is in possession of property, having acquired it for value (i.e., paid consideration) without knowing that such property was acquired through corrupt means or as proceeds of an offence under this Act. Such a transferee must establish both the payment of value and the absence of knowledge of the tainted nature of the property to claim protection from forfeiture.
definitions.plain_english: A bona fide transferee is someone who genuinely bought or received property by paying a fair price, without knowing that the property was originally obtained through corruption or bribery. Think of it as an innocent buyer who had no idea the seller got the property through illegal means. If such a person can prove they paid for it and had no knowledge of wrongdoing, the court cannot take away that property from them.
real_world_examples: A homebuyer in Noida purchases a flat from a government officer for Rs. 80 lakhs at market rate, not knowing the officer acquired it using bribe money; if the court later seeks to forfeit the flat, the buyer can claim bona fide transferee status by showing the registered sale deed and full payment.

A private company in Mumbai buys a commercial plot from a public servant through a registered transaction at circle rate, unaware that the servant had used proceeds of criminal misconduct to purchase it originally; the company can resist forfeiture by proving it paid full consideration in good faith.

A family in Chennai purchases agricultural land from a retired IAS officer through a documented sale at market value; when the CBI later attaches all assets of the officer, the family demonstrates they had no knowledge of corruption and paid legitimate consideration, qualifying as bona fide transferees.

A bank in Hyderabad acquires mortgaged property through an auction following loan default by a public servant later found guilty under the Prevention of Corruption Act; the bank can establish it was a bona fide transferee for value as it followed due legal process without knowledge of the property's tainted origin.

An individual in Kolkata purchases a vehicle from a Sub-Registrar accused of corruption, having obtained a clean RC and paid the full market price via bank transfer; when the Special Court considers forfeiture, the individual successfully establishes bona fide transferee status by producing payment records and demonstrating no prior knowledge of wrongdoing.
what_it_covers: A person who purchased property from a public servant at market value through a registered transaction, having no knowledge of its corrupt origins.
A financial institution that acquired property through a lawful auction or mortgage enforcement process without awareness that the original owner obtained it via bribery or criminal misconduct.

A family member or third party who received property as part of a legitimate commercial sale, paid full consideration, and can demonstrate through documentary evidence the absence of knowledge about the property's tainted nature.

A company that purchased immovable or movable assets from a person later charged under the Act, provided the transaction was at arm's length and there was no reason to suspect the corrupt origin of the asset.
what_it_excludes: A person who acquired property as a gift or without paying any consideration, since the definition requires transfer 'for value'.
A person who had actual knowledge or reasonable notice that the property was acquired through corrupt means or bribery, even if they paid market value for it.
A family member or associate of the accused public servant who received property as a sham or nominal transaction designed to shield assets from forfeiture, lacking genuine independent consideration.
A person who acquired property at a grossly undervalued price in circumstances that would put a reasonable person on notice of its suspicious or tainted origin.
An 'associated person' or someone acting in collusion with the corrupt public servant to launder property through a fictitious transfer.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person qualifies as a bona fide transferee is the decisive factor that blocks the Special Court from issuing a forfeiture order under Section 17D(2) of the Act — if established, it creates an absolute bar to forfeiture regardless of the property's tainted origin. Failure to meet this standard means the property will be forfeited to the State, making the burden of proof on the transferee critically important in corruption-related asset recovery proceedings.

definitions.definition: "Business" includes a trade or profession or providing service.
definitions.plain_english: The word 'business' in this law is given a wide meaning — it covers not just buying and selling goods (trade), but also professional activities like law or medicine, and any kind of service being offered or rendered. So whether a company sells products, provides consultancy, runs a hospital, or offers IT services, all of these count as 'business' under this law. The broad definition ensures that commercial organisations across all sectors are covered.
real_world_examples: An IT services company based in Bengaluru bribes a government official to secure a software development contract from a public sector undertaking — the company's 'business' of providing IT services falls squarely within this definition.

A chartered accountancy firm in Mumbai pays an undue advantage to a tax official to obtain favourable treatment for its clients — the firm's professional services constitute 'business' under Section 9.

A private hospital chain in Delhi offers a kickback to a public health department officer to be empanelled under a government health scheme — providing medical services is a 'business' covered by this definition.

A construction company in Hyderabad gives money to a municipal corporation official to retain a road-laying contract — the company's trade and contracting activity qualifies as 'business' for the purposes of Section 9.

A logistics and freight forwarding firm in Chennai bribes a customs official to expedite clearance of goods — its commercial operations as a service provider constitute 'business' within the meaning of this section.

A private security agency in Pune associated with a government-contracted facility management project pays an undue advantage to a public servant to retain the contract — providing security services is a 'business' under this definition.
what_it_covers: Trade activities — buying, selling, importing, exporting goods by a commercial organisation
Professional services — legal, medical, accounting, engineering, architectural or consultancy services rendered by a firm or body
Service-based activities — IT services, logistics, security, facility management, financial services, hospitality and similar service-sector operations
Mixed commercial operations — entities engaged in both manufacturing/trade and providing ancillary services
Businesses operating outside India — where a body incorporated in India carries on trade, profession or service in foreign jurisdictions
what_it_excludes: Activities of a purely personal or private nature not carried on for commercial gain, such as an individual's hobby or personal investment unconnected to any commercial organisation
Functions of government bodies or statutory authorities acting in a public capacity, since they are not 'commercial organisations' carrying on a 'business' for the purposes of Section 9
Charitable or not-for-profit activities where no trade, profession or service is being commercially rendered — though the boundary may depend on the actual conduct and structure of the entity
Isolated personal transactions by an individual that are not performed on behalf of or in the course of a commercial organisation's trade, profession or service
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an activity qualifies as 'business' under Section 9 is critical because it determines whether a commercial organisation can be held liable and punished with a fine for bribery of a public servant — without this nexus, the corporate offence under Section 9 cannot be established. The definition also governs the scope of the 'adequate procedures' defence available to commercial organisations, making compliance obligations relevant only where the entity is engaged in business as defined.

definitions.definition: "Commercial organisation" means (a) a body incorporated in India which carries on a business, whether in India or outside India; (b) any other body incorporated outside India which carries on a business, or part of a business, in any part of India; (c) a partnership firm or any association of persons formed in India which carries on a business whether in India or outside India; or (d) any other partnership or association of persons formed outside India which carries on a business, or part of a business, in any part of India.
definitions.plain_english: A commercial organisation is any company, partnership, or group of persons that runs a business — whether registered in India or abroad — as long as it either operates in India or was formed in India. This includes Indian companies doing business overseas and foreign companies doing even a small part of their business on Indian soil. Essentially, if an entity is in the business of trade, profession, or providing services and has a meaningful connection to India, it qualifies.
real_world_examples: A private limited company registered under the Companies Act in Mumbai that manufactures pharmaceuticals and exports them to Southeast Asia — it is incorporated in India and carries on business, so it is a commercial organisation under the Act.

A Singapore-incorporated multinational corporation that operates a back-office services centre in Bengaluru — because it carries on part of its business in India, it falls within the definition even though it is incorporated abroad.

A partnership firm of chartered accountants registered in Delhi under the Indian Partnership Act that provides audit and consultancy services — it is a partnership formed in India carrying on a profession (which counts as 'business'), making it a commercial organisation.

A foreign LLP incorporated in the United Kingdom that has a project management office in Hyderabad handling infrastructure contracts in India — its Indian operations bring it squarely within the definition.

An association of persons (such as a joint venture consortium) formed in India by several construction companies to bid for a highway project — even without separate incorporation, such an association carrying on business qualifies as a commercial organisation.

An e-commerce company incorporated in the Cayman Islands but operating its entire marketplace and fulfilment network within India — the conduct of business in India triggers the definition regardless of the foreign place of incorporation.
what_it_covers: Indian-incorporated private and public limited companies carrying on business anywhere in the world.
Foreign corporations (including MNCs) that conduct any part of their business operations within India, regardless of where they are registered.
Partnership firms and Limited Liability Partnerships (LLPs) formed in India engaged in trade, profession, or service provision.
Associations of persons formed in India (such as joint ventures or consortia) that undertake commercial activities.
Overseas partnerships or associations of persons that carry on business or part of their business in any part of India.
what_it_excludes: Government bodies, statutory corporations, and public sector undertakings acting in a purely sovereign or governmental capacity, as they are typically treated as public servants rather than commercial organisations.
Individuals acting in their personal capacity — the definition covers only bodies, firms, or associations, not sole proprietors or natural persons acting alone.
Non-profit organisations, trusts, and NGOs that do not carry on any trade, profession, or commercial service, since 'business' is a prerequisite of the definition.
Foreign entities that have absolutely no business activity or presence — even indirect — in India, as the territorial nexus to India is a required element.
Charitable or religious societies registered solely for non-commercial purposes with no profit-making or service-providing activity.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an entity qualifies as a 'commercial organisation' determines whether it can be prosecuted and fined under Sections 8 and 9 for bribery of public servants by associated persons, and whether its directors, managers, or officers can face individual imprisonment under Section 10. Without satisfying this definition, neither the organisational fine nor the personal liability of key managerial personnel under the Prevention of Corruption Act can be triggered.

definitions.definition: For the purposes of Section 19, 'competent authority' means the authority competent to remove a public servant from his office, being (i) the Central Government, in the case of a person employed in connection with the affairs of the Union who is not removable save by or with the sanction of the Central Government; (ii) the State Government, in the case of a person employed in connection with the affairs of a State who is not removable save by or with the sanction of the State Government; or (iii) such other authority as is competent to remove the concerned public servant from his office in any other case.
definitions.plain_english: The 'competent authority' is the government body or official that has the power to dismiss or remove a particular government employee from their job. Before a court can even begin hearing a corruption case against a public servant, this authority must first give its permission. Depending on who employs the public servant — the Central Government, a State Government, or some other body — the competent authority changes accordingly.
real_world_examples: An IAS officer posted in a Union Ministry is accused of accepting bribes; since only the Central Government can remove an IAS officer, the Central Government is the competent authority that must grant sanction before a court can take cognizance of the case.

A State PWD engineer employed by the Maharashtra Government is alleged to have demanded kickbacks for awarding road contracts; the Maharashtra State Government, being the authority competent to remove him, must grant prosecution sanction as the competent authority.

A municipal corporation employee in Chennai is accused of criminal misconduct; since he is removable by the municipal corporation (not the Central or State Government), the municipal corporation acts as the competent authority for granting sanction.

A judge of a High Court who cannot be removed without Presidential action — and by extension the approval of the Chief Justice of India — means the appropriate constitutional authority fulfils the role of competent authority for sanction purposes.

A retired IPS officer is prosecuted for an offence allegedly committed during his service tenure; under the Explanation to Section 19, the Central Government remains the competent authority based on who could have removed him at the time the offence was committed, not at the time of prosecution.

Where doubt arises whether a paramilitary officer's case falls under Central or State jurisdiction, Section 19(2) requires the authority that would have been competent to remove him at the time of the alleged offence to grant the sanction.
what_it_covers: The Central Government, when the accused public servant is employed in connection with Union affairs and is removable only by or with the sanction of the Central Government.
The State Government, when the accused public servant is employed in connection with State affairs and is not removable without the sanction of that State Government.

Any other authority (such as a municipal corporation, university governing body, or public sector undertaking board) that holds the power to remove the accused public servant from his post, in cases not falling under the Central or State Government categories.
The authority that was competent to remove the public servant at the time the alleged offence was committed, even if the servant has since retired, resigned, or been transferred to a different post.
The authority responsible for granting or refusing sanction within the prescribed timeline of three months (extendable by one month for legal consultation) after receiving a proposal for prosecution.
what_it_excludes: Courts themselves, which are expressly prohibited from taking cognizance without the competent authority's prior sanction and thus cannot act as the competent authority.

Private citizens or complainants, who cannot directly approach the competent authority for sanction unless they have first filed a complaint in a competent court and the court has directed them to obtain sanction.
Police officers or officers of investigating agencies acting in their individual capacity, as distinct from the institutional authority vested with removal power over the accused public servant.
Any authority that may have supervisory or disciplinary oversight over the public servant but does not hold the specific legal power to remove that servant from office.
The Lokpal or Lokayuktas in cases where the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 otherwise provides, as Section 19 expressly carves out those situations from its sanction requirement.
definitions.why_it_matters: Without the competent authority's prior sanction, no court can take cognizance of offences under Sections 7, 11, 13, and 15 of the Prevention of Corruption Act against a public servant, making the identification of the correct competent authority a threshold prerequisite that can entirely block or enable a prosecution. An error in identifying or approaching the wrong authority can render the entire prosecution void unless it is shown that a failure of justice has actually occurred.

definitions.definition: Confiscation, as used in the Prevention of Corruption Act, refers to the permanent transfer of title and ownership of money or property procured by means of an offence under the Act to the State, pursuant to an order made by a Special Judge, following the procedure prescribed under the Criminal Law Amendment Ordinance, 1944 (Ord. 38 of 1944). It operates as a final judicial order extinguishing all rights of the offender or associated persons in the property, distinct from and consequent upon attachment.
definitions.plain_english: Confiscation means the government permanently takes away money or property that a corrupt official or person gained through bribery or corruption. Unlike a temporary freeze (attachment), confiscation is a final court order that transfers full ownership of that property to the State. The corrupt person loses all rights to that property forever. This happens after a Special Judge passes an order under the applicable law.
real_world_examples: A senior IAS officer in Maharashtra accepts bribes worth ₹2 crore to award public construction contracts. After conviction, the Special Judge orders confiscation of the ₹2 crore deposited across multiple bank accounts, permanently transferring ownership to the State.

A government procurement officer in Delhi receives gratification in the form of a luxury apartment in Gurugram. Following a CBI investigation and trial, the Special Judge issues a confiscation order, and the apartment is permanently vested in the government.

A municipal engineer in Chennai is found to have procured gold jewellery and foreign currency through corrupt means. Upon conviction under the Prevention of Corruption Act, the Special Judge orders confiscation of all such assets identified as proceeds of the offence.

A state government employee in Uttar Pradesh deposits bribe money into a shell company account. The Special Judge, applying Criminal Law Amendment Ordinance, 1944 procedures, orders confiscation of the funds in that account after establishing they were procured through the corrupt offence.

An officer of a public sector undertaking in Kolkata is convicted for criminal misconduct after accepting undue advantage in exchange for awarding contracts. The court issues a confiscation order for vehicles and movable property purchased with bribe proceeds, vesting them in the State.
what_it_covers: Money deposited in bank accounts that was directly procured through bribery or criminal misconduct under the Act.

definitions.definition: Corrupt means, as used in Section 7A of the Prevention of Corruption Act, refers to any dishonest, fraudulent, or improper method or mode of inducement employed to influence a public servant to perform or forbear from performing a public duty improperly or dishonestly, including the use of bribery, deception, misrepresentation, or any other unlawful inducement that is not sanctioned by law. It encompasses means that are inherently tainted by dishonesty or illegality and are directed at subverting the impartial discharge of official functions.
definitions.plain_english: Corrupt means refers to any dishonest or unlawful method used to influence a government official into doing something improper or failing to do their duty. This could include offering bribes, using deception, or applying pressure through illegitimate channels. Essentially, it covers any underhanded tactic that corrupts the normal, honest functioning of a public servant. It is distinct from lawful persuasion or legitimate official communication.
real_world_examples: A contractor in Mumbai secretly pays a middleman to bribe a municipal building inspector to approve a substandard construction plan that should have been rejected — the payment to the middleman as an inducement to influence the inspector constitutes use of corrupt means.

A person in Delhi arranges for a third party to threaten a government licensing officer with exposure of unrelated personal information unless the officer fast-tracks a rejected licence application — the use of blackmail to influence the officer qualifies as corrupt means.

A businessman in Chennai fabricates false documents and channels money through a proxy to convince a tax official to reduce a legitimate tax liability, thereby using deception and financial inducement as corrupt means to influence the official's public duty.

An accused in a criminal case in Kolkata passes cash through a series of intermediaries to a court clerk to influence the clerk's superior (a public servant) into misplacing crucial case files — the layered financial inducement used to subvert official functioning constitutes corrupt means.

A real estate developer in Hyderabad funds a lavish overseas trip for a municipal councillor's family as a disguised reward to induce the councillor to vote in favour of an illegal rezoning proposal, thereby using corrupt means to influence the exercise of public duty.

Employing blackmail, coercion, or threat of exposure of personal information as a tool to compel a public servant to deviate from lawful official conduct.
Funnelling financial inducements through intermediaries specifically to cause a public servant to exercise official functions in a corrupt or dishonest manner.
Using informal back-channel payments, kickbacks, or hidden rewards to motivate a government official to approve, reject, or overlook matters under their official authority.
what_it_excludes: Lawful and legitimate lobbying, official representations, or written petitions submitted through proper legal channels to influence administrative decisions.

Exercise of personal influence through social or professional relationships not accompanied by any financial inducement or unlawful pressure — this is separately addressed under Section 7A as 'personal influence' and not treated as corrupt means.
Honest and transparent requests made directly to a public servant for expeditious processing of a matter, without any inducement, reward, or improper motive.

Actions of the public servant himself in accepting or soliciting bribes — the term 'corrupt means' under Section 7A governs the conduct of the person inducing the public servant, not the public servant's own corrupt act under separate provisions.
Legal remuneration or payments made to a public servant that are authorised by law and do not carry any improper motive or condition for deviating from official duty.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether conduct qualifies as 'corrupt means' under Section 7A is decisive in establishing the guilt of a person who induces a public servant to act improperly, triggering mandatory minimum imprisonment of three years extendable to seven years along with a fine. If the means used are not corrupt or illegal, and do not constitute personal influence, the essential ingredient of the offence under Section 7A fails and no conviction can be sustained.

definitions.definition: For the purposes of proceedings under the Prevention of Corruption Act, the Court of the special Judge shall be deemed to be a Court of Session, such that the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, applicable to a Court of Session shall apply to proceedings before the special Judge. This deeming fiction is operative under Section 5(3) of the Act and is further extended under Section 27 for the purposes of appeal and revision by the High Court.
definitions.plain_english: A 'Court of Session' in this law refers to the court of the special Judge, which is treated as if it were a Sessions Court for the purpose of applying criminal procedure rules. This legal fiction means that all the rights, procedures, and powers that normally apply in a Sessions Court also apply when a special Judge hears corruption cases. It does not mean the special Judge is literally a Sessions Judge, but the law treats the court as equivalent for procedural purposes.
real_world_examples: When a public servant in Maharashtra is tried before a special Judge under the Prevention of Corruption Act, the defense can invoke rights available in a Sessions Court trial under the CrPC, such as the right to examine witnesses and cross-examine prosecution witnesses, because the special Judge's court is deemed a Court of Session.

The High Court of Delhi exercises its powers of appeal and revision over a special Judge's conviction order in a bribery case as if it were reviewing a Sessions Court judgment, enabling the convict to file an appeal directly before the High Court under this deeming provision.

In a case involving a Central Government officer in Chennai being tried by a special Judge for criminal misconduct, the prosecution is conducted by a public prosecutor — as would be required in a Court of Session — because Section 5(3) equates the special Judge's court to a Court of Session.

A special Judge in Kolkata applies Section 326 of the CrPC (which governs transfer of cases partly heard) to a corruption trial, as permitted by Section 5(4), because the special Judge is simultaneously deemed a Magistrate for that specific provision — illustrating how the deeming provisions work selectively alongside the Court of Session fiction.

When an accused in a Prevention of Corruption case in Bengaluru seeks bail pending trial, the application is heard with reference to bail provisions applicable to Sessions Courts, since the special Judge's court is deemed a Court of Session under Section 5(3) of the Act.
what_it_covers: The court of the special Judge constituted under the Prevention of Corruption Act, which is deemed a Court of Session for all procedural purposes under the CrPC.
All proceedings before the special Judge where CrPC provisions applicable to a Court of Session are invoked, including bail, framing of charges, and examination of witnesses.
The exercise by the High Court of appellate and revisional jurisdiction over the special Judge's court as if it were a Sessions Court trying cases within the local limits of that High Court.
The conduct of prosecution before the special Judge by a public prosecutor, as mandated by the deeming of the court as a Court of Session under Section 5(3).
what_it_excludes: An actual Sessions Court presided over by a Sessions Judge or Additional Sessions Judge under the CrPC — the deeming is a legal fiction and does not make the special Judge a Sessions Judge in fact.
Proceedings before a Magistrate's court or other subordinate criminal courts that do not have special jurisdiction under the Prevention of Corruption Act.
The specific provisions of Section 326 and Section 475 of the CrPC for which the special Judge is separately deemed to be a Magistrate under Section 5(4), not a Court of Session.
Civil courts or tribunals, which fall entirely outside the scope of this deeming provision relating to criminal procedure.
definitions.why_it_matters: The deeming of the special Judge's court as a Court of Session determines which CrPC procedural provisions govern the trial, affects the mode of appeal and revision available to accused and prosecution, and ensures that a public prosecutor — rather than a private counsel — must conduct the case, thereby directly impacting the conduct, rights, and outcomes of corruption prosecutions under the Act.

definitions.definition: A public servant is said to commit the offence of criminal misconduct if he dishonestly or fraudulently misappropriates or otherwise converts for his own use any property entrusted to him or any property under his control as a public servant or allows any other person so to do; or if he intentionally enriches himself illicitly during the period of his office, including by being in possession of pecuniary resources or property disproportionate to his known sources of income which he cannot satisfactorily account for.
definitions.plain_english: Criminal misconduct means when a government official either steals or misuses public money or property in their care, or becomes richer than their legitimate salary and income can explain. If a public servant has assets or cash far beyond what their official income allows, the law presumes they acquired it through corrupt means. This is one of the most serious corruption offences a government employee can commit in India.
real_world_examples: A municipal corporation engineer in Maharashtra diverts funds allocated for road construction into his personal bank account and awards the project to a contractor who pays him a kickback — constituting misappropriation of entrusted property.

An Income Tax officer in Delhi is found, during a raid, to possess benami properties, jewellery, and fixed deposits worth ₹15 crore, while his total lawful salary income over his service period amounts to only ₹60 lakh — a classic case of possession of disproportionate assets.

A state government treasury official in Uttar Pradesh manipulates records to transfer public funds to a shell company owned by his relative, thereby converting government property under his control for another person's use.

A district collector in Telangana, entrusted with relief funds for flood victims, siphons off ₹2 crore into accounts linked to his family members, constituting both misappropriation and illicit enrichment.

A senior officer in a public sector bank in Karnataka approves fraudulent loans to fictitious borrowers and receives a percentage of disbursed amounts, resulting in criminal misconduct as the property under his official control is converted for his personal gain.

A food supply officer in Punjab is found holding agricultural land registered in his wife's name purchased during his posting period at values far exceeding his known salary, triggering the disproportionate assets presumption under Section 13.
what_it_covers: A public servant who dishonestly misappropriates money or property entrusted to him in his official capacity for personal use.
A public servant who allows another person (such as a relative or associate) to misappropriate or convert property that is under the public servant's official control.

A public servant who, during the period of his office, is found to possess pecuniary resources or property disproportionate to his known sources of income and cannot satisfactorily explain the excess.
Intentional illicit enrichment of a public servant through any act of omission or commission during the tenure of his office, even if no specific act of misappropriation is directly proved.
Attempts to commit the misappropriation variant of criminal misconduct, which are independently punishable under Section 15.
what_it_excludes: Mere negligence or inefficiency by a public servant in handling public funds or property, without dishonest or fraudulent intent, does not constitute criminal misconduct.

Legitimate income, gifts received in accordance with applicable government rules, or inherited wealth that a public servant can satisfactorily account for is excluded from the ambit of disproportionate assets.

Acts of bribery or demanding undue advantage by a public servant, which are governed separately under Section 7 and related provisions, are not subsumed within the definition of criminal misconduct under Section 13.
Private individuals or persons who are not public servants cannot commit the offence of criminal misconduct under this section, even if they abet or benefit from it.

Property held by a public servant prior to the commencement of his office period, if legitimately acquired and satisfactorily accounted for, falls outside the scope of disproportionate assets scrutiny.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act qualifies as criminal misconduct under Section 13 determines whether the public servant faces mandatory minimum imprisonment of four years extendable to ten years along with fine; it also directly triggers the power of property attachment and seizure under Section 17C, governs the framing of charges under Section 23, and makes attempts to commit such acts punishable under Section 15.

definitions.definition: The Delhi Special Police Establishment, as used in Section 17 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, refers to the central investigative police agency established under the Delhi Special Police Establishment Act, 1946, which functions under the Central Government and is commonly known as the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI). In the context of this Act, it denotes that police officers of this establishment, at the rank of Inspector of Police or above, are authorised to investigate offences punishable under this Act.
definitions.plain_english: The Delhi Special Police Establishment (DSPE) is the central government's premier investigative agency, better known as the CBI. It is a special police force set up by a separate central law and operates across India, unlike state police forces which are limited to their own states. When it comes to investigating corruption cases, only an Inspector of Police or a higher-ranking officer from this agency can investigate without needing prior court permission.
real_world_examples: A CBI Inspector investigates a corruption case against a senior central government officer accused of accepting bribes in a defence procurement contract, exercising authority under Section 17 without requiring a Magistrate's prior order.

The DSPE/CBI takes up investigation of a Railways ministry official alleged to have demanded gratification for awarding a construction tender, with an Inspector of Police leading the probe as the minimum permissible rank under the Prevention of Corruption Act.

A CBI Sub-Inspector attempts to investigate a corruption allegation against a public servant but is stopped because under Section 17, only an Inspector or above within the DSPE is authorised to do so, making the Sub-Inspector's actions invalid.

In a high-profile case involving disproportionate assets of an IAS officer, the DSPE registers an FIR and assigns the case to an Inspector of Police, who proceeds to make an arrest without a warrant under the authority conferred by Section 17.

The DSPE investigates a bank fraud-linked corruption matter involving a public sector bank official, where the Inspector-rank officer coordinates with the Superintendent of Police before investigating offences falling under Section 13(1)(b) of the Act, as required by the second proviso to Section 17.
what_it_covers: Officers of the CBI (Central Bureau of Investigation) functioning under the Delhi Special Police Establishment Act, 1946, at the rank of Inspector of Police and above, authorised to investigate corruption offences under this Act.

CBI Inspectors and senior officers who may investigate offences punishable under the Prevention of Corruption Act without the prior order of a Metropolitan Magistrate or Magistrate of the first class.
CBI officers of Inspector rank or above who are empowered to make arrests in corruption cases without a warrant, subject to the conditions of Section 17.
Investigation of offences under Section 13(1)(b) by DSPE officers of at least Superintendent of Police rank, as mandated by the second proviso to Section 17.
what_it_excludes: State police officers, even if they hold the rank of Inspector, as they do not belong to the Delhi Special Police Establishment and are governed by the separate rank thresholds specified in Section 17 for metropolitan areas or other areas.
CBI officers below the rank of Inspector of Police, such as Sub-Inspectors or Constables, who are not authorised to investigate or make arrests under Section 17 of the Prevention of Corruption Act.

Officers of other central agencies such as the Enforcement Directorate, Income Tax Investigation Wing, or Serious Fraud Investigation Office, who are not part of the Delhi Special Police Establishment.
Private investigative agencies or vigilance officers of public sector undertakings, who have no authority under this provision regardless of their designation or rank.
definitions.why_it_matters: The classification of a police force as the Delhi Special Police Establishment directly determines the minimum rank of officer permitted to investigate corruption offences under Section 17, setting it at Inspector of Police rather than the Deputy Superintendent of Police rank required elsewhere, thereby affecting the validity of the investigation and any consequent arrest. If an investigation is conducted by a DSPE officer below the prescribed rank without a Magistrate's order, it may result in failure of justice or render the investigation procedurally invalid, potentially undermining the prosecution.

Examples: A CBI Inspector investigates a corruption case against a senior central government officer accused of accepting bribes in a defence procurement contract, exercising authority under Section 17 without requiring a Magistrate's prior order. | The DSPE/CBI takes up investigation of a Railways ministry official alleged to have demanded gratification for awarding a construction tender, with an Inspector of Police leading the probe as the minimum permissible rank under the Prevention of Corruption Act. | A CBI Sub-Inspector attempts to investigate a corruption allegation against a public servant but is stopped because under Section 17, only an Inspector or above within the DSPE is authorised to do so, making the Sub-Inspector's actions invalid. | In a high-profile case involving disproportionate assets of an IAS officer, the DSPE registers an FIR and assigns the case to an Inspector of Police, who proceeds to make an arrest without a warrant under the authority conferred by Section 17. | The DSPE investigates a bank fraud-linked corruption matter involving a public sector bank official, where the Inspector-rank officer coordinates with the Superintendent of Police before investigating offences falling under Section 13(1)(b) of the Act, as required by the second proviso to Section 17.

Tags: central investigative agency, CBI investigative authority, minimum rank for investigation, anti-corruption enforcement body, Inspector of Police threshold, central government police establishment, special police force corruption probe, DSPE jurisdiction under PCA, federal investigative police unit, authorised investigating officer rank

Covers: Officers of the CBI (Central Bureau of Investigation) functioning under the Delhi Special Police Establishment Act, 1946, at the rank of Inspector of Police and above, authorised to investigate corruption offences under this Act.; CBI Inspectors and senior officers who may investigate offences punishable under the Prevention of Corruption Act without the prior order of a Metropolitan Magistrate or Magistrate of the first class.; CBI officers of Inspector rank or above who are empowered to make arrests in corruption cases without a warrant, subject to the conditions of Section 17.; Investigation of offences under Section 13(1)(b) by DSPE officers of at least Superintendent of Police rank, as mandated by the second proviso to Section 17.

Excludes: State police officers, even if they hold the rank of Inspector, as they do not belong to the Delhi Special Police Establishment and are governed by the separate rank thresholds specified in Section 17 for metropolitan areas or other areas.; CBI officers below the rank of Inspector of Police, such as Sub-Inspectors or Constables, who are not authorised to investigate or make arrests under Section 17 of the Prevention of Corruption Act.; Officers of other central agencies such as the Enforcement Directorate, Income Tax Investigation Wing, or Serious Fraud Investigation Office, who are not part of the Delhi Special Police Establishment.; Private investigative agencies or vigilance officers of public sector undertakings, who have no authority under this provision regardless of their designation or rank.

Why it matters: The classification of a police force as the Delhi Special Police Establishment directly determines the minimum rank of officer permitted to investigate corruption offences under Section 17, setting it at Inspector of Police rather than the Deputy Superintendent of Police rank required elsewhere, thereby affecting the validity of the investigation and any consequent arrest. If an investigation is conducted by a DSPE officer below the prescribed rank without a Magistrate's order, it may result in failure of justice or render the investigation procedurally invalid, potentially undermining the prosecution.

definitions.definition: The 'Designated Authority' means the authority notified by the Government of Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir before whom properties seized or attached under section 17C are produced, and who is empowered to confirm or revoke orders of seizure or attachment, grant or refuse permission to deal with such property, and who exercises all the powers of a civil court for making a full and fair enquiry into the matter.
definitions.plain_english: The Designated Authority is a specific official or body appointed by the Jammu and Kashmir UT Government to oversee properties that have been seized or frozen during a corruption investigation. This authority acts as an independent check on the investigating officer — it can either approve or cancel the freezing of assets and decides whether someone can use or transfer their seized property. It works like a quasi-judicial body, meaning it can hold hearings and take evidence like a court.
real_world_examples: A Deputy Superintendent of Police in J&K's Anti-Corruption Bureau seizes a government contractor's bank accounts and vehicles suspected to be proceeds of a bribery scam; the Investigating Officer notifies the Designated Authority within 48 hours, who then holds a hearing and either confirms or cancels the attachment order.

A public servant in Jammu whose property has been attached under section 17C applies to the Designated Authority seeking permission to sell his attached house to pay for his children's education; the Designated Authority evaluates the request and grants or refuses permission after considering the case merits.

An ACB officer in Srinagar attaches a plot of land belonging to a corrupt revenue official and notifies the Designated Authority by placing the report at its disposal, upon which the immovable property is deemed 'produced' before the authority for further proceedings.

During a live investigation, the Investigating Officer believes a corrupt officer may hurriedly transfer his assets; he issues a provisional 90-day restraint order and immediately seeks ratification from the Designated Authority, which then holds a hearing with both the officer and the accused before making a final decision.

A person aggrieved by the Designated Authority's order confirming attachment of his commercial property in J&K appeals to the Special Judge under section 17D, who reviews the Designated Authority's reasoned order and either upholds or revokes it within 60 days.
semantic_tags: civil court powers in corruption cases
what_it_covers: The authority notified by the Government of Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir specifically empowered to receive production of seized or attached properties under section 17C.

Proceedings where the Designated Authority confirms or revokes an order of seizure or attachment within thirty days after affording a hearing to both the Investigating Officer and the affected person.
Applications by aggrieved persons seeking permission to transfer or deal with attached property, which the Designated Authority adjudicates using civil court powers.
Cases where the Investigating Officer notifies the Designated Authority within 48 hours of seizure or attachment along with a full circumstantial report.

Supervision and safety of attached or seized property until disposal of the case, including immovable property where a written notification by the Investigating Officer substitutes physical production.
what_it_excludes: The Special Judge or Special Court, who operates at the appellate stage under section 17D and is a distinct authority from the Designated Authority.

The Director of the Anti-Corruption Bureau, whose role is limited to granting prior written approval for seizure orders and does not perform the quasi-judicial review functions of the Designated Authority.

Any authority constituted by a state government other than the Government of Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir, as the Designated Authority is exclusively notified by the UT government under this provision.
The Investigating Officer himself, who initiates and reports the seizure or attachment but has no power to confirm, revoke, or adjudicate on it in the manner reserved for the Designated Authority.
Courts of general criminal jurisdiction such as ordinary Magistrates or Sessions Courts, which have no role in confirming or revoking attachment orders under section 17C.
definitions.why_it_matters: The Designated Authority acts as a critical procedural safeguard in corruption cases: without its confirmation, an attachment or seizure order under section 17C may be revoked, restoring property to the accused and potentially undermining the prosecution; conversely, its confirmation secures the continued attachment of proceeds of criminal misconduct until final disposal, and its orders are directly appealable to the Special Court under section 17D, making it the pivotal first quasi-judicial arbiter of property rights in corruption investigations in J&K.

definitions.definition: For the purposes of Section 10, 'director', in relation to a firm, means a partner in the firm. In relation to a commercial organisation that is a company, a director refers to a person occupying the position of director on the board of such company, who may be held guilty of an offence under Section 9 where such offence is proved to have been committed with their consent or connivance.
definitions.plain_english: A 'director' is a person who holds a top decision-making role in a business organisation — such as a board director in a company or a partner in a partnership firm. If the organisation commits a bribery offence and it can be shown that this person agreed to it or turned a blind eye, they can be personally prosecuted. The law extends the meaning of 'director' to include partners in firms so that no one can escape responsibility by simply calling their business a 'firm' instead of a 'company'.
real_world_examples: A Managing Director of a Mumbai-based infrastructure company approves payments made to a government official to secure a public works contract. When the company is prosecuted under Section 9, the Managing Director is also personally charged under Section 10 as a 'director' who consented to the corrupt act.

Two partners of a Delhi law firm arrange for a payment to a public servant to influence a regulatory decision. Since the firm is a commercial organisation under the Act, each partner is treated as a 'director' and faces imprisonment of three to seven years along with a fine.

A non-executive director of a Bengaluru-based IT company is aware of a bribe being paid to a foreign government official to win a software procurement deal but takes no action to stop it. Courts examine whether this connivance makes her liable as a 'director' under Section 10.

The promoter-director of a Hyderabad pharmaceutical company sanctions payments described as 'consulting fees' to a public servant to obtain drug approvals. Both the company and the director are prosecuted, with the director facing a mandatory minimum sentence of three years.

A partner in a Kolkata trading firm personally negotiates an undue advantage for a customs official to clear an import shipment. Being a 'director' within the meaning of Section 10, the partner is individually liable even though the payment was made in the firm's name.
what_it_covers: A person formally appointed as a director on the board of a company that is a commercial organisation under the Act.
A partner in a partnership firm, explicitly included within the definition of 'director' for the purposes of Section 10.
A Managing Director or Whole-time Director of a private or public limited company who consents to or connives in the commission of an offence under Section 9.
A designated director in a Limited Liability Partnership (LLP) that qualifies as a commercial organisation, where that person exercises decision-making authority.
A shadow director or de facto director whose conduct demonstrates control over the commercial organisation's decisions relevant to the corrupt act.
what_it_excludes: Ordinary employees or staff of a commercial organisation who do not hold the position of director, manager, secretary or equivalent officer and are not partners in a firm.
Independent third parties or consultants who advise a commercial organisation but do not occupy a formal directorial or partnership role within it.
Public servants acting in their official capacity, who are governed by separate provisions of the Act and not by the corporate liability framework of Section 10.
Shareholders or investors in a company who have no directorial role, board seat, or involvement in day-to-day management decisions.
A director of a foreign company that does not qualify as a 'commercial organisation' within the jurisdictional scope of the Act.
definitions.why_it_matters: The definition of 'director' determines who among the leadership of a commercial organisation can be individually prosecuted and punished under Section 10 when the organisation itself commits an offence under Section 9, triggering mandatory imprisonment of not less than three years. By extending the term to include partners in firms, the Act ensures that the choice of business structure cannot be used to shield culpable individuals from personal criminal liability.

definitions.definition: The term 'dishonestly' is not separately defined in the Prevention of Corruption Act, but as used in Sections 7 and 13, it refers to conduct by a public servant carried out with the intent to cause wrongful gain or wrongful loss, or to act in bad faith in the performance or non-performance of a public duty, in a manner contrary to law, established procedure, or the honest discharge of official responsibility. It imports the meaning assigned to it under Section 24 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, denoting an act done with the intention of causing wrongful gain to one person or wrongful loss to another.
definitions.plain_english: Acting 'dishonestly' means a public servant deliberately does something they know is wrong — either to benefit themselves or someone else, or to harm someone unfairly — when carrying out their official duties. It is not an honest mistake or genuine error of judgment; it is an intentional, bad-faith act. For example, if a government officer misuses public funds kept in their charge knowing it is not theirs to use, that is acting dishonestly.
real_world_examples: A tehsildar in Uttar Pradesh deliberately records a land mutation in favour of a private party who paid him a bribe, knowing the legal owner has not consented and the transfer is invalid — this is dishonest performance of a public duty under Section 7.

A public works department engineer in Maharashtra approves inflated bills for a road construction contractor in exchange for a share of the excess amount, misappropriating government funds entrusted to him — constituting dishonest misappropriation under Section 13(1)(a).

A passport office clerk in Delhi deliberately delays a legitimately complete application and marks it deficient in the system, then demands money to 'correct' the status, acting dishonestly to extract an undue advantage under Section 7.

A state treasury officer in Tamil Nadu diverts government funds meant for a welfare scheme into a private account accessible to him, knowingly converting property entrusted to him for personal use — a dishonest act under Section 13.

A ration shop dealer (fair price shop owner) holding a public distribution licence in Bihar deliberately issues less than the entitled quantity of subsidised grain and sells the balance in the open market, dishonestly misappropriating property under his control as a public servant.

A municipal corporation inspector in Kolkata, entrusted with demolition records, dishonestly certifies that an unauthorised construction has been demolished while accepting payment from the builder to spare the structure — dishonest performance of public duty under Section 7.
what_it_covers: A public servant who intentionally misappropriates or diverts government funds or property entrusted to him, knowing such appropriation is unauthorised, under Section 13(1)(a).

A public servant who performs an official act — such as granting a licence, approving a file, or issuing a certificate — in a manner he knows to be contrary to rules or facts, in exchange for or in anticipation of an undue advantage, under Section 7.
A public servant who deliberately withholds or delays a legitimate public service with the conscious intent to extract a payment, thereby performing his duty dishonestly.
Any act by a public servant that involves intentional misrepresentation, falsification of records, or knowing deviation from prescribed procedure to cause wrongful gain or loss.
what_it_excludes: Genuine errors of judgment or bona fide mistakes made by a public servant acting in good faith, even if the decision turns out to be wrong or causes loss.
Actions taken by a public servant under a reasonable but mistaken interpretation of law or procedure, where there is no intent to cause wrongful gain or loss.
Mere negligence or administrative lapses where the public servant did not consciously intend to act contrary to duty or to benefit any particular person.
Acts that are procedurally irregular but performed transparently and openly without any concealment or intent to deceive, and without personal benefit.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act is done 'dishonestly' is a core element of the offences under Sections 7 and 13 of the Prevention of Corruption Act — its presence determines whether a public servant's conduct constitutes a punishable offence attracting imprisonment of three to ten years, or whether it remains a mere administrative irregularity. Without establishing the dishonest intent, the prosecution cannot secure a conviction for criminal misconduct or bribery under the Act.
